name: Young v. County of Los Angeles
court: Ninth Circuit (from the Central District of California, District Judge Manuel L. Real)
topic: Fourth Amendment excessive force, pepper spray without warning and baton blows on a seatbelt violator who refused to get back in his truck and sat on the curb eating broccoli, pepper spray and baton blows held to be intermediate force, qualified immunity denied, order to reenter the vehicle held lawful
summary: A Los Angeles County deputy stopped a probation officer for a seatbelt violation. When the man got out of his truck, handed over his registration and then refused repeated orders to sit back in the truck, choosing to sit on the curb and eat his broccoli, the deputy pepper sprayed him from behind without warning and then struck him with a baton, including, on the plaintiff's account, once after he was face down on the ground. The Ninth Circuit held that pepper spray and baton blows are intermediate force, that on these facts the force was excessive, and that the deputy was not entitled to qualified immunity because Graham, Blankenhorn and Headwaters had long given notice that significant force cannot be used on a non-threatening, non-fleeing misdemeanant. It also held that an officer may lawfully order a driver back into the vehicle during a traffic stop.
coverage: The opinion by Judge Reinhardt, including all footnotes, was read in full from the Ninth Circuit's archive at https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2011/08/26/09-56372.pdf. The slip opinion carries docket No. 09-56372 and district court No. 2:08-cv-05438-R-RZ, filed August 26, 2011.

The slip opinion does not print its own Federal Reporter citation. The citation 655 F.3d 1156 is the one given in the course materials and the assignment and could not be confirmed from the source read. Chief Judge Kozinski's dissent in the Mattos en banc opinion (also read) cites this case by slip opinion page, which is consistent with its filing date but does not confirm the reporter page.
No subsequent history (petition for rehearing, remand proceedings) was checked.

The facts are stated as the court stated them on review of summary judgment, in the light most favorable to Young, with the factual disputes noted where the court noted them. The audio recording and the deputy's incident report are described only as the court described them.
facts:
Because the case was decided on summary judgment, the court took Young's version of the facts.

At about 10:22 a.m. one February morning in 2007, Mark Anthony Young, a 46 year old African-American probation officer, was driving his truck to the gym in workout clothes, eating a snack of broccoli and tomato, when Deputy Richard Wells of the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department pulled him over for driving without a seatbelt. An audio recording captured what followed. Young conceded the seatbelt violation and that his truck was missing a side mirror and a rear plate. He produced his license and insurance but could not immediately find his registration. Wells told him to keep looking and returned to his motorcycle to write the citation.

When Young found the registration he got out of the truck, carrying the registration and his vegetables, walked to the motorcycle, and handed it over. Wells told him to "just have a seat in the truck." Young said he did not feel like sitting in his truck, walked past it, sat on the sidewalk curb, and went back to eating. Wells repeated the order several times, finally saying that until Young sat in the truck he could not write the ticket. Young kept refusing.

Shortly afterward, while Young was still seated on the curb, Wells approached him from behind and pepper sprayed him. Young's declaration says he felt liquid on his head, turned, and saw Wells holding the can for the first time. The recording captures Young saying "You don't give me warning," and Wells answering, "I don't have to give you a warning." Wells kept spraying as Young rose and tried to back away. Young repeatedly protested that he was an officer of the law. According to Young, Wells then drew his baton, swung at his head eight or more times, which Young blocked with his arms, landed a solid blow to his shin, and ordered him to the ground. In the district court Wells said he struck Young because he believed Young was moving and circling to gain a position of advantage and was about to throw the broccoli as a distraction before assaulting him. On appeal Wells did not argue that either the spray or the baton was motivated by safety concerns.

Young did not immediately go down and kept objecting. A second deputy, Berk, arrived and ordered him to the ground; Young complied, was handcuffed, and Berk put a knee on his back. Young says Wells struck him with the baton again after he was on the ground. When Young complained the cuffs were too tight, Berk said that was "part of not going along with the program," and told him that if he kept getting agitated he would be pepper sprayed. After several minutes Young was allowed to stand and was placed in a patrol car. A footnote notes that Wells's incident report quoted Young saying "Fuck you, I don't want to, I'm eating my vegetables," a statement the audio does not contain.

Young sued Wells and the county for excessive force, false imprisonment and negligence. The district court granted summary judgment to the defendants on all claims.
holding:
Affirmed on false imprisonment, reversed on excessive force and negligence, and remanded. The court stated the rule that the use of intermediate force is unreasonable when an officer has detained a suspect for minor infractions and the suspect clearly poses no threat to the officer or public safety.

Nature of the intrusion. Pepper spray and baton blows are both forms of force capable of inflicting significant pain and causing serious injury, and both are intermediate force. Quoting Headwaters, the court described pepper spray as designed to cause intense pain, with burning, mucus discharge, involuntary eye closure, a gagging reflex, temporary paralysis of the larynx, and disorientation, anxiety and panic. Young's evidence included a retired sheriff's lieutenant's declaration that the California POST basic curriculum teaches that pepper spray can have very serious and debilitating consequences, should generally be used only as a defensive weapon, and must never be used to intimidate or retaliate; that California officers are taught the baton is a deadly weapon that can cause deep bruising and blood clots capable of precipitating deadly strokes and should be used only in response to aggressive or combative acts; and that department policy prohibits head strikes with an impact weapon unless deadly force is justified. The amount of force was significant: a spray lasting several seconds rather than a minimal burst, multiple swings at the head, and two blows to the legs, one while Young was restrained on the ground. Whatever label is used, the court said, such force must be justified by a commensurately serious state interest.

Governmental interest. The most important factor, immediate threat, decisively favored Young. Wells did not contend Young posed any threat before the spray, and could not: Young was sitting on the curb with his back turned, eating. As to the baton, Wells's incident report statements of fear were, at most, a jury question, because a simple statement of fear is not enough without objective factors, and because an officer's provocative conduct can trigger a limited right to offer reasonable resistance; a jury could easily conclude that moving and circling after being sprayed from behind without warning was a reasonable response, not a threat. A blow delivered while Young lay face down would exceed any safety concern. Severity: a seatbelt infraction and a non-violent section 148(a)(1) misdemeanor. When disobedience takes the form of passive noncompliance that creates minimal disturbance and indicates no threat, it will not, without more, create a governmental interest in significant force. Resistance and flight: Young was not being arrested and was not fleeing; Wells sprayed him before even warning that he could be arrested, and said and did nothing that could be taken as initiating an arrest before the baton. Alternatives: Wells could have warned of arrest, warned that force would follow, simply attempted to handcuff him, or waited for the assistance he had apparently called for. He chose none, which showed how limited the government's interest was.

Balance. The force was significant and the interest minimal, so on Young's facts the force was excessive. The court added that it is rarely if ever necessary to use substantial force without warning against a person suspected only of minor offenses who is not resisting arrest and poses no apparent threat, and noted Headwaters II had found pepper spray excessive in such circumstances even with a warning.

Qualified immunity. Graham's balancing and the Ninth Circuit's criteria were long established before 2007. Blankenhorn had held in 2007, about conduct in 2001, that Graham's principle that force is justified only when there is a need for force put officers on notice that gang tackling a relatively calm, non-resisting trespass suspect without trying less violent means was unconstitutional. Headwaters II had held that pepper spraying a non-violent misdemeanant who disobeys an order but poses no threat is excessive. Those holdings gave Wells specific and unambiguous notice. A footnote adds that the POST training evidence supports the conclusion but the holding rests on constitutional law. The denial of immunity on summary judgment was reversed.

False imprisonment. Extending United States v. Williams from passengers to drivers, the court held that an officer issuing a citation does not violate the Fourth Amendment by ordering a driver to reenter the vehicle for the duration of the stop. Young's refusal was therefore a section 148(a)(1) violation, not protected speech, and Wells had authority to arrest, so the false imprisonment claim failed. Because the Fourth Amendment violation also establishes a breach of the duty of care under California law, the negligence claim was reinstated.
notDecided:
Whether Wells actually used excessive force. The court held only that, on Young's version of the facts, the force was excessive and the law clearly established, so summary judgment was improper. The case was remanded for trial.

How many baton blows were struck. The court held that was a jury question and that even two blows, one on the ground, would raise a genuine issue.

Whether Wells's claimed fear of an assault was credible or reasonable. The court held that was for the jury.

Any separate municipal defense of the county. The county rested on the argument that the claims against Wells failed, so the court's rulings applied to both without addressing municipal liability doctrine.

Whether an order to reenter a vehicle is lawful outside the traffic stop context. The holding is limited to a driver during a traffic stop while a citation is being issued.
inPractice:
Young is the case to read whenever a traffic stop turns into a contest of wills. The deputy had the law on his side right up to the moment he used force: the court held the order to get back in the truck was lawful and that Young's refusal was an arrestable misdemeanor. What the deputy did not have was a reason for intermediate force. A man sitting on a curb with his back to you, eating, is not a threat, and refusing to sit in a truck is passive noncompliance, not active resistance.

The court listed the alternatives it expected: tell him he will be arrested if he does not comply, tell him force will be used, go hands on to handcuff, or wait for the backup already called. The deputy skipped all four and went to spray and then baton. The recorded exchange, in which the deputy said he did not have to give a warning, became evidence against him.

The case also shows how training standards reach the courtroom. The plaintiff's expert put POST's own description of pepper spray and the baton into the record, along with the department's rule against head strikes absent deadly force justification, and the court used that material to describe the level of force and to say the conduct violated basic police practice.

Finally, Young explains the provocation doctrine officers should know: a person sprayed from behind without warning who stands up and moves is not necessarily resisting, and a jury may see the officer's own conduct as having started the struggle.

Dr. Sowards teaches Young with Bryan and Headwaters in the less lethal line, and in the impact weapons course for the baton holding.
trainIt:
Teach the escalation ladder the court described. Before any intermediate tool on a non-compliant, non-threatening subject, students should be able to show they warned of arrest, warned of force, attempted a hands-on arrest if safe, or waited for backup, or explain why none was feasible. Script the scenario exactly as it happened: lawful stop, lawful order, refusal, subject seated and eating. Grade the student on the words used before any tool comes out.

Teach the baton as the court described it. Young's evidence was that California officers are taught the baton is a deadly weapon that can cause deep bruising and blood clots capable of precipitating deadly strokes, and that it is for aggressive or combative acts. Head strikes were barred by department policy absent deadly force justification. Students should be able to name the target areas, the prohibited areas, and the level of resistance that justifies a strike, and should understand that a strike on a handcuffed or prone subject will be judged as force far beyond any safety need.

Teach pepper spray the same way. POST's curriculum, as described in the opinion, treats it as a defensive weapon that must never be used to intimidate or retaliate. A several second spray from behind on a seated person, followed by continued spraying as he backs away, does not fit that description.

Teach the recording. The deputy's words were on tape and in the opinion. Students should assume every stop is recorded and that "I don't have to give you a warning" will be read aloud in court.

Teach the posture: summary judgment reversed on the plaintiff's facts, remand for trial, no finding that the deputy was liable. The lawful order holding and the excessive force holding are separate, and students should be able to explain how an arrest can be lawful and the force used to make it still unconstitutional.
caution: The reporter citation 655 F.3d 1156 could not be confirmed from the slip opinion and is taken from the course materials. All facts are Young's version as the court was required to view them on summary judgment; the deputy's report and summary judgment papers described a threatening subject, and the court left those disputes to a jury. The opinion decides that a jury could find excessive force and that immunity was unavailable; it does not find that force was in fact excessive.

applications.title: Pepper spray and the baton are intermediate force
applications.body: Both are capable of significant pain and serious injury and both require a commensurately serious interest. The court used POST's own curriculum and the department's head strike policy to describe how serious these tools are.

applications.title: A lawful order does not license force
applications.body: The order to get back in the truck was lawful and the refusal was a misdemeanor. The force question is separate. Passive noncompliance that creates minimal disturbance and no threat does not, without more, justify significant force.

applications.title: Name the alternative you skipped
applications.body: Warn of arrest, warn of force, attempt to handcuff, or wait for backup. The court listed all four as feasible and reasonable. Choosing none of them showed how limited the government's interest in significant force was.

applications.title: Your own conduct can start the fight
applications.body: Spraying a seated man from behind without warning could be provocative conduct that triggers a limited right to reasonable resistance. A jury may see his standing and moving as a reaction, not an attack.

applications.title: Nothing after control
applications.body: A baton blow while the subject lies face down and handcuffed, if the jury believes it happened, exceeds any safety concern, reasonable or otherwise.

applications.title: Posture
applications.body: Summary judgment for the deputy was reversed on the excessive force and negligence claims and affirmed on false imprisonment. The case went back for trial. The court did not find the deputy liable.

quiz.q: What did the court hold about the deputy's order that Young get back in his truck?
options: It was unlawful because Young was the driver, not a passenger
It was lawful: an officer issuing a citation may order a driver to reenter the vehicle for the duration of the stop, so Young's refusal violated Penal Code section 148(a)(1)
It was lawful only because Young was a probation officer
The court did not decide the question
quiz.teach: The court extended its reasoning in United States v. Williams from passengers to drivers and affirmed summary judgment on the false imprisonment claim. The lawfulness of the order did not decide the separate question of whether the force used was reasonable.

quiz.q: Which less intrusive alternatives did the court say were feasible before the deputy used pepper spray?
options: None; the court said the deputy had to use force or abandon the stop
Warning Young he would be arrested, warning that force would be used, attempting to handcuff him, or waiting for the assistance he had called for
Only writing the ticket and leaving
quiz.teach: The court rejected the argument that the deputy's only options were to abandon the order or use force, listing four feasible and reasonable alternatives and holding that bypassing all of them showed how limited the government's interest in significant force was.

quiz.q: On what basis did the court hold that the law was clearly established in 2007?
options: Graham's principle that force is justified only by a need for force, as applied in Blankenhorn (gang tackle of a calm trespass suspect) and Headwaters II (pepper spray on non-violent protesters who disobeyed orders)
quiz.teach: The court said Blankenhorn had found the same principle clearly established for conduct in 2001, and that Headwaters II gave specific notice that pepper spray on a non-threatening misdemeanant who disobeys an order is excessive. The POST evidence supported the conclusion but the holding rested on constitutional law.
